questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Compute radial velocity from Doppler shift
questions.stem: A spectral line at 500 nm is shifted by 0.6 nm; the radial velocity in km/s is:

options.misconception: treats the wavelength shift itself as a speed

questions.explanation: The Doppler relation v = c times the shift over the rest wavelength gives about 360 km/s. A wavelength shift in nanometers is not itself a velocity.
questions.hint: Divide the shift by the rest wavelength, then multiply by light speed.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Compared with a 1 m telescope, a 3.0 m telescope gathers how many times more light?

options.misconception: uses the diameter ratio without squaring

questions.explanation: Collecting area scales with the square of the aperture, so a 3.0 m mirror gathers about 9 times the light of a 1 m mirror.
questions.hint: Area goes as diameter squared.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: An asteroid orbits the Sun at 0.5 AU; its orbital period in years is:

options.misconception: uses the semi-major axis as the period
squares instead of using the three-halves power

questions.explanation: Kepler's third law says period squared equals semi-major axis cubed, so P is a to the 3/2 power, about 0.35 years at 0.5 AU.
questions.hint: P squared equals a cubed for solar orbits.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A comet has an orbital period of 2.5 years; its semi-major axis in AU is:

options.misconception: uses the period itself as the distance
uses the square root of the period

questions.explanation: Rearranging Kepler's third law gives a equals P to the two-thirds power, about 1.84 AU for a period of 2.5 years.
questions.hint: Take the two-thirds power of the period.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Infer central mass from an orbit
questions.stem: A moon orbits with semi-major axis 3 AU and period 1 yr; the central mass in solar masses is:
questions.explanation: Newton's form gives central mass as a cubed divided by P squared in solar units, which is 27.00 here. A shorter period at the same distance implies a larger mass.
questions.hint: Mass equals a cubed over P squared.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A world with 3 Earth masses and 1 Earth radii has density about how many times Earth's?

options.misconception: forgets that volume scales with radius cubed
multiplies by radius instead of dividing
squares the radius instead of cubing it

questions.explanation: Density is mass over volume, and volume grows as radius cubed, so the ratio is 3 over 1 cubed, about 3.00. Larger worlds are not automatically denser.
questions.hint: Volume scales as radius to the third power.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A world with 3 Earth masses and 1 Earth radii has surface gravity about how many times Earth's?

options.misconception: multiplies by radius instead of dividing
cubes the radius in the denominator

questions.explanation: Surface gravity scales as mass over radius squared, giving 3.00 times Earth's for 3 masses and 1 radii. A big radius can offset a large mass.
questions.hint: Gravity follows the inverse-square law in radius.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: The solar flux at 0.75 AU, given 1361 W/m2 at 1 AU, is about:

options.misconception: multiplies by distance instead of dividing
uses the square of distance in the numerator

questions.explanation: Flux falls as the square of distance, so at 0.75 AU it is 1361 divided by 0.75 squared, about 2420 W/m2. This is why distant planets are colder.
questions.hint: Flux drops with the square of distance.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: If fusion converts 2.0 million tonnes each second, the Sun's output is about how many times 10^26 J per second?

options.misconception: ignores the factor of c squared entirely
uses ten times the correct conversion
misplaces the decimal by one place

questions.explanation: Einstein's E equals m c squared, and a million tonnes is 10^9 kg, so 2.0 million tonnes yields about 1.80 times 10^26 J each second.
questions.hint: One million tonnes is 10^9 kilograms.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the Sun's remaining life
questions.stem: At 3 Gyr old, how much longer has the Sun on the main sequence?

options.misconception: overstates the elapsed time instead of the remainder
assumes the full lifetime still remains
adds the age to the total lifetime

questions.explanation: Subtracting the current age from the total main-sequence lifetime gives 10 minus 3, about 7 Gyr left before the Sun leaves the main sequence.
questions.hint: Remaining life is total lifetime minus current age.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Relate distance to light travel time
questions.stem: Sunlight takes about 5.8 minutes to reach a planet at 0.7 AU from the Sun:

options.misconception: uses the fixed one-AU travel time
adds distance to the travel time

questions.explanation: Light takes about 8.3 minutes to cross 1 AU, so at 0.7 AU the travel time is 5.8 minutes. Looking outward in space is also looking back in time.
questions.hint: One astronomical unit is about 8.3 light-minutes.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star at 40 pc has a distance modulus m minus M of about:

options.misconception: uses parsecs instead of ten-parsec reference

questions.explanation: Distance modulus equals 5 times log of distance in parsecs over 10, giving 3.01 for 40 pc. It links apparent and absolute magnitude.
questions.hint: The reference distance in the formula is 10 parsecs.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with radius 1.5 solar radii and temperature 3200 K has luminosity about how many Suns?

options.misconception: uses temperature squared instead of to the fourth

questions.explanation: Relative luminosity follows radius squared times temperature-to-the-fourth, giving 0.21 Suns. Temperature has a much stronger effect than radius.
questions.hint: Luminosity scales as R squared times T to the fourth.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with absolute magnitude 2.2 is about how many times more luminous than the Sun at 4.83?
questions.explanation: Luminosity ratio is 2.512 raised to the Sun's magnitude minus the star's, about 11.27. Lower absolute magnitude means intrinsically brighter.
questions.hint: A difference of five magnitudes is a factor of 100.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with surface temperature 3200 K belongs to which spectral class?

options.misconception: assigns a class meant for hotter stars
assigns a class meant for cooler stars

questions.explanation: The sequence O B A F G K M runs from hot to cool, and 3200 K falls in class K. Spectral class tracks surface temperature, not stellar mass directly.
questions.hint: O is hottest and M is coolest.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A main-sequence star of 0.7 solar masses has luminosity about how many Suns?

options.misconception: uses mass squared instead of the steep power
uses an exponent that is too shallow

questions.explanation: For main-sequence stars luminosity scales roughly as mass to the 3.5 power, giving 0.3 Suns at 0.7 solar masses. Massive stars burn far brighter and shorter.
questions.hint: Luminosity rises much faster than mass.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A 0.9 solar-mass star stays on the main sequence about how many Gyr?

options.misconception: uses a simple inverse of mass
uses inverse-square instead of the steep exponent

questions.explanation: Lifetime scales as 10 Gyr times mass to the minus 2.5, which is 13.01 Gyr here. Massive stars exhaust fuel quickly despite having more of it.
questions.hint: Lifetime falls steeply as mass rises.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Predict the fate of a white dwarf
questions.stem: A stellar remnant of 1.60 solar masses exceeds the 1.4 solar-mass limit; it will likely:

options.misconception: ignores that the mass limit has been exceeded

options.text: collapse straight into a black hole
options.misconception: confuses a thermonuclear blast with direct collapse

options.text: reignite hydrogen fusion in a shell
options.misconception: reverses the direction of stellar evolution

questions.explanation: Above about 1.4 solar masses electron degeneracy cannot support a white dwarf, so carbon ignition produces a supernova. Stable existence is impossible at 1.60 solar masses.
questions.hint: Electron degeneracy fails above 1.4 solar masses.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Match initial mass to a remnant
questions.stem: A star born with 2.0 solar masses will most likely:

options.misconception: assigns a low-mass outcome to a high-mass star
assumes the star never leaves the main sequence

questions.explanation: Initial mass decides the endpoint: under about 8 solar masses gives a white dwarf, 8 to 20 gives a neutron star, and above that a black hole. At 2.0 solar masses the corresponding remnant follows.
questions.hint: Very massive stars leave the densest remnants.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Find distance from a supernova magnitude
questions.stem: A Type Ia supernova with apparent magnitude 8.30 and absolute magnitude -19.3 lies about how many Mpc away?
questions.explanation: Distance modulus is m minus M, here 27.60, which converts to 0.03 Mpc. Type Ia supernovae are standardizable candles because their peak luminosity is similar.
questions.hint: Distance modulus relates apparent and absolute magnitude.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy at 35 Mpc recedes at about how many km/s, taking H0 as 70?
questions.explanation: Hubble's law gives recession speed as H0 times distance, about 2450 km/s at 35 Mpc. It describes the average expansion flow, not peculiar motions.
questions.hint: Velocity equals Hubble constant times distance.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy with redshift 0.015 has recession speed about how many km/s?

options.misconception: treats the dimensionless redshift as a speed

questions.explanation: At small redshift, v is approximately c times z, giving about 4500 km/s. Redshift itself has no units and is not a velocity.
questions.hint: For small z, velocity is c times z.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A line rest at 500 nm appears at 514 nm; the redshift is:
questions.explanation: Redshift is observed minus rest wavelength over rest wavelength, which is 0.028 here. Dividing by the observed wavelength gives a different, incorrect quantity.
questions.hint: Always divide the shift by the rest wavelength.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy rotating at 40 km/s at 10 kpc has mass about how many times 10^10 solar masses?

options.misconception: uses speed rather than speed squared
drops the radius from the expression

questions.explanation: Balancing gravity and circular motion gives mass as v squared times radius over G, about 0.4 times 10^10 solar masses. Flat rotation curves imply large dark halos.
questions.hint: Mass follows from v squared times r over G.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy of apparent magnitude 8.2 at 12 Mpc has absolute magnitude about:

options.misconception: adds the distance modulus instead of subtracting
uses megaparsecs where parsecs are needed

questions.explanation: Absolute magnitude is apparent magnitude minus the distance modulus, giving -22.20 for 8.2 at 12 Mpc. This removes the dimming due to distance.
questions.hint: Subtract five times log of distance in parsecs over ten.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: If the Hubble constant were 60.6 km/s/Mpc, the approximate age of the universe in Gyr would be:

options.misconception: uses the constant itself as an age

questions.explanation: The inverse Hubble constant sets the expansion timescale, about 16.1 Gyr for H of 60.6. The true age depends slightly on the universe's composition.
questions.hint: Age is roughly the inverse of the Hubble constant.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: At redshift 0.03, the cosmic scale factor a was about:

options.misconception: uses redshift directly as the scale factor

questions.explanation: The scale factor relates to redshift by a equals 1 over 1 plus z, which is 0.971 here. A smaller a means the universe was more compressed.
questions.hint: One plus redshift is the inverse scale factor.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: The CMB temperature at redshift 0.03, given 2.725 K today, is about:

options.misconception: omits the one in the expansion

questions.explanation: CMB temperature scales as 2.725 times 1 plus z, about 2.81 K here. The radiation cooled as the universe expanded.
questions.hint: Temperature grows in proportion to one plus redshift.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: If dark energy is 32% and dark matter is 63%, ordinary matter is about what percent?
questions.explanation: The components must sum to 100 percent, so ordinary matter is 100 minus 32 minus 63, about 5 percent. Most of the universe is not ordinary atoms.
questions.hint: All cosmic components add up to 100 percent.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Infer planet size from transit depth
questions.stem: A planet 3 Earth radii crossing a 0.5 solar-radius star dims it by about what percent?

options.misconception: uses the radius ratio without squaring
uses a linear conversion to solar radii

questions.explanation: Transit depth equals the area ratio, so 3 Earth radii against 0.5 solar radii gives about 0.30 percent. Deeper transits imply larger planets.
questions.hint: Depth is the square of the radius ratio.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with luminosity 0.35 Suns has its habitable zone near what distance in AU?

options.misconception: squares luminosity instead of taking root

questions.explanation: Habitable-zone distance scales as the square root of luminosity, about 0.59 AU here. Brighter stars push the zone farther out.
questions.hint: Distance scales as the square root of luminosity.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A planet at 0.07 AU around a solar-mass star has an orbital period of about how many days?

options.misconception: uses a cubed without the root
uses the square root of a

questions.explanation: Kepler's third law gives period in years as a to the 3/2 power, or 7 days at 0.07 AU. Close-in planets have very short years.
questions.hint: Period in years is a to the three-halves power.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A 0.5 Jupiter-mass planet at 0.15 AU around a solar-mass star induces a reflex speed near how many m/s?

options.misconception: uses distance instead of inverse square root

questions.explanation: The reflex speed scales as 28 m/s times planet mass divided by the square root of distance, giving 36 m/s. Bigger, closer planets make bigger wobbles.
questions.hint: Speed falls as the square root of orbital distance.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Scale signal to noise with exposure
questions.stem: A 1-hour exposure reaches SNR 10; a 4-hour exposure reaches about:

options.misconception: assumes signal to noise grows linearly
adds exposure time to the ratio

questions.explanation: For photon noise, signal to noise grows as the square root of exposure time, so 4 hours gives about 20.0. Four times the time doubles the ratio.
questions.hint: Signal to noise improves as the square root of time.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star counted at 985 photons/s versus a reference at 1000 photons/s is fainter by how many magnitudes?

options.misconception: uses the raw count ratio as magnitudes

questions.explanation: Magnitude difference is 2.5 times log of the reference count over the target count, about 0.02. The magnitude scale compresses large flux ratios.
questions.hint: Use 2.5 times the base-ten logarithm.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: An interferometer with baseline 30 m at 500 nm resolves about how many milliarcseconds?

options.misconception: uses the baseline as an angle

questions.explanation: Angular resolution is wavelength over baseline, about 3.44 milliarcseconds here. Longer baselines resolve far finer detail than a single dish.
questions.hint: Resolution improves as the baseline grows.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Two independent errors of 3 and 1 combine in quadrature to about:
questions.explanation: Independent uncertainties add in quadrature, the square root of 3 squared plus 1 squared, about 3.16. Linear addition overstates the combined error.
questions.hint: Square, add, then take the square root.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A photon of wavelength 116 nm has energy about how many electronvolts?
questions.explanation: Photon energy in electronvolts is 1240 divided by wavelength in nanometers, about 10.69 eV here. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy per photon.
questions.hint: Energy and wavelength are inversely related.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: An object spans 2.5 arcminutes on the sky; its angular size in degrees is:

options.misconception: treats arcminutes as if they were degrees
uses arcseconds per degree by mistake
multiplies by sixty instead of dividing

questions.explanation: There are 60 arcminutes in one degree, so dividing 2.5 by 60 gives 0.042 degrees. Treating arcminutes as degrees skips that conversion entirely.
questions.hint: A degree contains 60 arcminutes.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Star A at magnitude 1 outshines star B at magnitude 5 by what factor?

treats each magnitude as a factor of one hundred
halves the magnitude step before exponentiating

questions.explanation: A difference of 4 magnitudes corresponds to 2.512 raised to 4, about 39.82 times brighter. The magnitude difference alone is logarithmic, not a brightness ratio.
questions.hint: Each five magnitudes is a factor of 100.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star has a parallax of 3.5 milliarcseconds; its distance in parsecs is:

options.misconception: mistakes the parallax angle for the distance
multiplies the angle by 1000 instead of dividing

questions.explanation: Distance in parsecs equals 1000 divided by parallax in milliarcseconds, giving 285.71 pc. Parallax is a small angle and shrinks as the star gets farther away.
questions.hint: One parsec is the distance with one arcsecond of parallax.

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star rises at 6:03 tonight; about how many minutes earlier will it rise tomorrow night?

options.misconception: confuses the 24-hour solar day with the shift
uses a full hour as the nightly advance
assumes stars rise at the same clock time

questions.explanation: A sidereal day is roughly four minutes shorter than a solar day, so a star rises about four minutes earlier each night. That is why constellations drift through the seasons.
questions.hint: The sidereal day is about 23h 56m.

questions.stem: When the Moon is 28 degrees from the Sun, the illuminated fraction is about:

takes the angle fraction as the lit fraction
forgets to halve the geometric factor

questions.explanation: The sunlit fraction of the lunar disk is (1 minus cos of the elongation) over 2, which gives 0.06 here. At full moon the elongation is 180 degrees and the fraction reaches one.
questions.hint: Full moon means an elongation of 180 degrees.

uses the pole's declination of ninety

questions.explanation: Declination measures angular distance north or south of the celestial equator, so a value of +4 means 4 degrees north. The north celestial pole itself sits at +90 degrees.
questions.hint: Declination is measured from the celestial equator.

questions.stem: If fusion converts 2.5 million tonnes each second, the Sun's output is about how many times 10^26 J per second?

options.misconception: ignores the factor of c squared entirely
uses ten times the correct conversion
misplaces the decimal by one place

questions.explanation: Einstein's E equals m c squared, and a million tonnes is 10^9 kg, so 2.5 million tonnes yields about 2.25 times 10^26 J each second.
questions.hint: One million tonnes is 10^9 kilograms.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Reason about the Sun's remaining life
questions.stem: At 4 Gyr old, how much longer has the Sun on the main sequence?

options.misconception: overstates the elapsed time instead of the remainder
assumes the full lifetime still remains
adds the age to the total lifetime

questions.explanation: Subtracting the current age from the total main-sequence lifetime gives 10 minus 4, about 6 Gyr left before the Sun leaves the main sequence.
questions.hint: Remaining life is total lifetime minus current age.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Relate distance to light travel time
questions.stem: Sunlight takes about 6.6 minutes to reach a planet at 0.8 AU from the Sun:

options.misconception: uses the fixed one-AU travel time
adds distance to the travel time

questions.explanation: Light takes about 8.3 minutes to cross 1 AU, so at 0.8 AU the travel time is 6.6 minutes. Looking outward in space is also looking back in time.
questions.hint: One astronomical unit is about 8.3 light-minutes.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star at 50 pc has a distance modulus m minus M of about:

options.misconception: uses parsecs instead of ten-parsec reference

questions.explanation: Distance modulus equals 5 times log of distance in parsecs over 10, giving 3.49 for 50 pc. It links apparent and absolute magnitude.
questions.hint: The reference distance in the formula is 10 parsecs.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with radius 2.0 solar radii and temperature 3300 K has luminosity about how many Suns?

options.misconception: uses temperature squared instead of to the fourth

questions.explanation: Relative luminosity follows radius squared times temperature-to-the-fourth, giving 0.43 Suns. Temperature has a much stronger effect than radius.
questions.hint: Luminosity scales as R squared times T to the fourth.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with absolute magnitude 2.3 is about how many times more luminous than the Sun at 4.83?
questions.explanation: Luminosity ratio is 2.512 raised to the Sun's magnitude minus the star's, about 10.28. Lower absolute magnitude means intrinsically brighter.
questions.hint: A difference of five magnitudes is a factor of 100.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with surface temperature 3300 K belongs to which spectral class?

options.misconception: assigns a class meant for hotter stars
assigns a class meant for cooler stars

questions.explanation: The sequence O B A F G K M runs from hot to cool, and 3300 K falls in class K. Spectral class tracks surface temperature, not stellar mass directly.
questions.hint: O is hottest and M is coolest.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A main-sequence star of 0.8 solar masses has luminosity about how many Suns?

options.misconception: uses mass squared instead of the steep power
uses an exponent that is too shallow

questions.explanation: For main-sequence stars luminosity scales roughly as mass to the 3.5 power, giving 0.5 Suns at 0.8 solar masses. Massive stars burn far brighter and shorter.
questions.hint: Luminosity rises much faster than mass.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A 1.1 solar-mass star stays on the main sequence about how many Gyr?

options.misconception: uses a simple inverse of mass
uses inverse-square instead of the steep exponent

questions.explanation: Lifetime scales as 10 Gyr times mass to the minus 2.5, which is 7.88 Gyr here. Massive stars exhaust fuel quickly despite having more of it.
questions.hint: Lifetime falls steeply as mass rises.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Predict the fate of a white dwarf
questions.stem: A stellar remnant of 1.65 solar masses exceeds the 1.4 solar-mass limit; it will likely:

options.misconception: ignores that the mass limit has been exceeded

options.text: collapse straight into a black hole
options.misconception: confuses a thermonuclear blast with direct collapse

options.text: reignite hydrogen fusion in a shell
options.misconception: reverses the direction of stellar evolution

questions.explanation: Above about 1.4 solar masses electron degeneracy cannot support a white dwarf, so carbon ignition produces a supernova. Stable existence is impossible at 1.65 solar masses.
questions.hint: Electron degeneracy fails above 1.4 solar masses.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Match initial mass to a remnant
questions.stem: A star born with 2.5 solar masses will most likely:

options.misconception: assigns a low-mass outcome to a high-mass star
assumes the star never leaves the main sequence

questions.explanation: Initial mass decides the endpoint: under about 8 solar masses gives a white dwarf, 8 to 20 gives a neutron star, and above that a black hole. At 2.5 solar masses the corresponding remnant follows.
questions.hint: Very massive stars leave the densest remnants.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Find distance from a supernova magnitude
questions.stem: A Type Ia supernova with apparent magnitude 8.45 and absolute magnitude -19.3 lies about how many Mpc away?
questions.explanation: Distance modulus is m minus M, here 27.75, which converts to 0.04 Mpc. Type Ia supernovae are standardizable candles because their peak luminosity is similar.
questions.hint: Distance modulus relates apparent and absolute magnitude.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy at 40 Mpc recedes at about how many km/s, taking H0 as 70?
questions.explanation: Hubble's law gives recession speed as H0 times distance, about 2800 km/s at 40 Mpc. It describes the average expansion flow, not peculiar motions.
questions.hint: Velocity equals Hubble constant times distance.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy with redshift 0.020 has recession speed about how many km/s?

options.misconception: treats the dimensionless redshift as a speed

questions.explanation: At small redshift, v is approximately c times z, giving about 6000 km/s. Redshift itself has no units and is not a velocity.
questions.hint: For small z, velocity is c times z.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A line rest at 500 nm appears at 516 nm; the redshift is:
questions.explanation: Redshift is observed minus rest wavelength over rest wavelength, which is 0.032 here. Dividing by the observed wavelength gives a different, incorrect quantity.
questions.hint: Always divide the shift by the rest wavelength.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy rotating at 50 km/s at 12 kpc has mass about how many times 10^10 solar masses?

options.misconception: uses speed rather than speed squared
drops the radius from the expression

questions.explanation: Balancing gravity and circular motion gives mass as v squared times radius over G, about 0.7 times 10^10 solar masses. Flat rotation curves imply large dark halos.
questions.hint: Mass follows from v squared times r over G.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A galaxy of apparent magnitude 8.3 at 13 Mpc has absolute magnitude about:

options.misconception: adds the distance modulus instead of subtracting
uses megaparsecs where parsecs are needed

questions.explanation: Absolute magnitude is apparent magnitude minus the distance modulus, giving -22.27 for 8.3 at 13 Mpc. This removes the dimming due to distance.
questions.hint: Subtract five times log of distance in parsecs over ten.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: If the Hubble constant were 60.9 km/s/Mpc, the approximate age of the universe in Gyr would be:

options.misconception: uses the constant itself as an age

questions.explanation: The inverse Hubble constant sets the expansion timescale, about 16.1 Gyr for H of 60.9. The true age depends slightly on the universe's composition.
questions.hint: Age is roughly the inverse of the Hubble constant.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: At redshift 0.04, the cosmic scale factor a was about:

options.misconception: uses redshift directly as the scale factor

questions.explanation: The scale factor relates to redshift by a equals 1 over 1 plus z, which is 0.962 here. A smaller a means the universe was more compressed.
questions.hint: One plus redshift is the inverse scale factor.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: The CMB temperature at redshift 0.04, given 2.725 K today, is about:

options.misconception: omits the one in the expansion

questions.explanation: CMB temperature scales as 2.725 times 1 plus z, about 2.83 K here. The radiation cooled as the universe expanded.
questions.hint: Temperature grows in proportion to one plus redshift.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: If dark energy is 33% and dark matter is 62%, ordinary matter is about what percent?
questions.explanation: The components must sum to 100 percent, so ordinary matter is 100 minus 33 minus 62, about 5 percent. Most of the universe is not ordinary atoms.
questions.hint: All cosmic components add up to 100 percent.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Infer planet size from transit depth
questions.stem: A planet 4 Earth radii crossing a 0.5 solar-radius star dims it by about what percent?

options.misconception: uses the radius ratio without squaring
uses a linear conversion to solar radii

questions.explanation: Transit depth equals the area ratio, so 4 Earth radii against 0.5 solar radii gives about 0.54 percent. Deeper transits imply larger planets.
questions.hint: Depth is the square of the radius ratio.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with luminosity 0.45 Suns has its habitable zone near what distance in AU?

options.misconception: squares luminosity instead of taking root

questions.explanation: Habitable-zone distance scales as the square root of luminosity, about 0.67 AU here. Brighter stars push the zone farther out.
questions.hint: Distance scales as the square root of luminosity.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A planet at 0.09 AU around a solar-mass star has an orbital period of about how many days?

options.misconception: uses a cubed without the root
uses the square root of a

questions.explanation: Kepler's third law gives period in years as a to the 3/2 power, or 10 days at 0.09 AU. Close-in planets have very short years.
questions.hint: Period in years is a to the three-halves power.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A 0.6 Jupiter-mass planet at 0.20 AU around a solar-mass star induces a reflex speed near how many m/s?

options.misconception: uses distance instead of inverse square root

questions.explanation: The reflex speed scales as 28 m/s times planet mass divided by the square root of distance, giving 38 m/s. Bigger, closer planets make bigger wobbles.
questions.hint: Speed falls as the square root of orbital distance.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Scale signal to noise with exposure
questions.stem: A 1-hour exposure reaches SNR 10; a 5-hour exposure reaches about:

options.misconception: assumes signal to noise grows linearly
adds exposure time to the ratio

questions.explanation: For photon noise, signal to noise grows as the square root of exposure time, so 5 hours gives about 22.4. Four times the time doubles the ratio.
questions.hint: Signal to noise improves as the square root of time.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star counted at 980 photons/s versus a reference at 1000 photons/s is fainter by how many magnitudes?

options.misconception: uses the raw count ratio as magnitudes

questions.explanation: Magnitude difference is 2.5 times log of the reference count over the target count, about 0.02. The magnitude scale compresses large flux ratios.
questions.hint: Use 2.5 times the base-ten logarithm.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: An interferometer with baseline 40 m at 500 nm resolves about how many milliarcseconds?

options.misconception: uses the baseline as an angle

questions.explanation: Angular resolution is wavelength over baseline, about 2.58 milliarcseconds here. Longer baselines resolve far finer detail than a single dish.
questions.hint: Resolution improves as the baseline grows.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Two independent errors of 4 and 1 combine in quadrature to about:
questions.explanation: Independent uncertainties add in quadrature, the square root of 4 squared plus 1 squared, about 4.12. Linear addition overstates the combined error.
questions.hint: Square, add, then take the square root.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A photon of wavelength 124 nm has energy about how many electronvolts?
questions.explanation: Photon energy in electronvolts is 1240 divided by wavelength in nanometers, about 10.00 eV here. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy per photon.
questions.hint: Energy and wavelength are inversely related.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: An object spans 3.0 arcminutes on the sky; its angular size in degrees is:

options.misconception: treats arcminutes as if they were degrees
uses arcseconds per degree by mistake
multiplies by sixty instead of dividing

questions.explanation: There are 60 arcminutes in one degree, so dividing 3.0 by 60 gives 0.050 degrees. Treating arcminutes as degrees skips that conversion entirely.
questions.hint: A degree contains 60 arcminutes.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Star A at magnitude 1 outshines star B at magnitude 6 by what factor?

options.misconception: uses the magnitude difference itself as a factor
treats each magnitude as a factor of one hundred
halves the magnitude step before exponentiating

questions.explanation: A difference of 5 magnitudes corresponds to 2.512 raised to 5, about 100.02 times brighter. The magnitude difference alone is logarithmic, not a brightness ratio.
questions.hint: Each five magnitudes is a factor of 100.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star has a parallax of 4.0 milliarcseconds; its distance in parsecs is:

options.misconception: mistakes the parallax angle for the distance
multiplies the angle by 1000 instead of dividing

questions.explanation: Distance in parsecs equals 1000 divided by parallax in milliarcseconds, giving 250.00 pc. Parallax is a small angle and shrinks as the star gets farther away.
questions.hint: One parsec is the distance with one arcsecond of parallax.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star rises at 6:04 tonight; about how many minutes earlier will it rise tomorrow night?

options.misconception: confuses the 24-hour solar day with the shift
uses a full hour as the nightly advance
assumes stars rise at the same clock time

questions.explanation: A sidereal day is roughly four minutes shorter than a solar day, so a star rises about four minutes earlier each night. That is why constellations drift through the seasons.
questions.hint: The sidereal day is about 23h 56m.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: When the Moon is 35 degrees from the Sun, the illuminated fraction is about:

options.misconception: uses the wrong sign for the cosine term
takes the angle fraction as the lit fraction
forgets to halve the geometric factor

questions.explanation: The sunlit fraction of the lunar disk is (1 minus cos of the elongation) over 2, which gives 0.09 here. At full moon the elongation is 180 degrees and the fraction reaches one.
questions.hint: Full moon means an elongation of 180 degrees.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star at declination +5 degrees lies how many degrees north of the celestial equator?

options.misconception: uses the complement to the pole instead
uses the pole's declination of ninety

questions.explanation: Declination measures angular distance north or south of the celestial equator, so a value of +5 means 5 degrees north. The north celestial pole itself sits at +90 degrees.
questions.hint: Declination is measured from the celestial equator.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A star with surface temperature 3400 K peaks near what wavelength in nanometers?
questions.explanation: Wien's law puts the peak near 2.9 million divided by 3400 kelvin, about 852.9 nm. Hotter blackbodies peak at shorter, bluer wavelengths.
questions.hint: Peak wavelength times temperature is roughly constant.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A 0.9 m telescope observing at 550 nm has a diffraction limit in arcseconds of:
questions.explanation: The diffraction limit is 1.22 times wavelength over aperture, which for 0.9 m gives 0.15 arcseconds. Larger mirrors resolve finer detail because the angle shrinks with diameter.
questions.hint: Resolution improves as aperture increases.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Compute radial velocity from Doppler shift
questions.stem: A spectral line at 500 nm is shifted by 1.0 nm; the radial velocity in km/s is:

options.misconception: treats the wavelength shift itself as a speed

questions.explanation: The Doppler relation v = c times the shift over the rest wavelength gives about 600 km/s. A wavelength shift in nanometers is not itself a velocity.
questions.hint: Divide the shift by the rest wavelength, then multiply by light speed.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: Compared with a 1 m telescope, a 4.0 m telescope gathers how many times more light?

options.misconception: uses the diameter ratio without squaring

questions.explanation: Collecting area scales with the square of the aperture, so a 4.0 m mirror gathers about 16 times the light of a 1 m mirror.
questions.hint: Area goes as diameter squared.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: An asteroid orbits the Sun at 0.7 AU; its orbital period in years is:

options.misconception: uses the semi-major axis as the period
squares instead of using the three-halves power

questions.explanation: Kepler's third law says period squared equals semi-major axis cubed, so P is a to the 3/2 power, about 0.59 years at 0.7 AU.
questions.hint: P squared equals a cubed for solar orbits.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A comet has an orbital period of 3.5 years; its semi-major axis in AU is:

options.misconception: uses the period itself as the distance
uses the square root of the period

questions.explanation: Rearranging Kepler's third law gives a equals P to the two-thirds power, about 2.31 AU for a period of 3.5 years.
questions.hint: Take the two-thirds power of the period.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.learningObjective: Infer central mass from an orbit
questions.stem: A moon orbits with semi-major axis 5 AU and period 1 yr; the central mass in solar masses is:
questions.explanation: Newton's form gives central mass as a cubed divided by P squared in solar units, which is 125.00 here. A shorter period at the same distance implies a larger mass.
questions.hint: Mass equals a cubed over P squared.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A world with 5 Earth masses and 1 Earth radii has density about how many times Earth's?

options.misconception: forgets that volume scales with radius cubed
multiplies by radius instead of dividing
squares the radius instead of cubing it

questions.explanation: Density is mass over volume, and volume grows as radius cubed, so the ratio is 5 over 1 cubed, about 5.00. Larger worlds are not automatically denser.
questions.hint: Volume scales as radius to the third power.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: A world with 5 Earth masses and 1 Earth radii has surface gravity about how many times Earth's?

options.misconception: multiplies by radius instead of dividing
cubes the radius in the denominator

questions.explanation: Surface gravity scales as mass over radius squared, giving 5.00 times Earth's for 5 masses and 1 radii. A big radius can offset a large mass.
questions.hint: Gravity follows the inverse-square law in radius.

provenance.author: bank-team-astronomy
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ASTRONOMY
questions.stem: The solar flux at 0.95 AU, given 1361 W/m2 at 1 AU, is about:

options.misconception: multiplies by distance instead of dividing
uses the square of distance in the numerator

questions.explanation: Flux falls as the square of distance, so at 0.95 AU it is 1361 divided by 0.95 squared, about 1508 W/m2. This is why distant planets are colder.
questions.hint: Flux drops with the square of distance.
